#1046. Jack Grealish absent from Everton squad again after disciplinary breach

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Grealish was left out of Everton’s Carabao Cup triumph against Newcastle on Thursday as punishment for skipping Everton training when he was not authorised to do so

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Jack Grealish has been left out of Everton’s squad again following an internal disciplinary breach as the Toffees face Newcastle in the Premier League.

Grealish was not part of the travelling party to Tyneside for Everton’s second meeting with the Magpies in the space of five days, with David Moyes’ side emerging 3-1 victors when the teams clashed in the Carabao Cup at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday.

The 31-year-old winger was absent for that match as punishment for skipping Everton training when he was not authorised to do so.

Grealish, who is in his second spell on loan at Everton, had been in contention to return after missing Everton’s defeat to Arsenal on Saturday, which was put down to illness.

Instead, manager David Moyes left him out of the squad altogether, preferring to name two goalkeepers on the bench for the visit of Matthias Jaissle’s side, and he has opted against including him once again Monday night’s trip to St James’ Park.

The club say this is down to the player not being match fit.

Moyes made two changes from the team that beat Newcastle last week, with Tyler Dibling and Hayden Hackney - who bagged a goal and an assist - dropping to the bench. Jarrad Branthwaite returns to the side, with Jake O’Brien moving to right-back and Merlin Rohl moving forward, while Harrison Armstrong starts alongside James Garner in midfield.

Grealish, who is in the last season of his contract at Manchester City, rejoined Everton on loan on transfer deadline day and has since made six appearances, failing to score.

#1045. Formula One in Rwanda: Sportswashing claims vs. hopes for African legacy

Formula One will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider African society.

Rwanda's sports portfolio has grown after confirming it will host Formula One races from the early 2030s. The track is to be built in Bugesera near Kigali International Airport, which Qatar Airways, an F1 sponsor, owns 60% of.

"To be an African and to see it happening in real time, for me in my lifetime because Kyalami [the track in South Africa where F1 was last hosted in Africa] was before I was born, I'm more than happy to have it on the continent," South African presenter and content creator Nqobile Khwezi told Sky Sports.

"To be able to give that taste back to the rest of the world and the audience of Formula One would be an absolute delight."

F1 have also highlighted the benefits for the host nation.

"Through this race we have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to our more than 100 million fans across Africa and firmly believe that sport can be a positive force for good," an F1 spokesperson told The Athletic.

DW contacted Rwanda's Ministry of Sports for comment, but did not receive a promised reply.

For the country's President, Paul Kagame, another move into sport is hardly a surprise given his ventures into European football and the NBA in recent years. Rwanda even sponsored Bayern Munich, but fan and media backlash over the deal caused the Bundesliga club to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year.

With many critics accusing Kagame and Rwanda of sportswashing, the arrival of F1, a sport valued at approximately $34 billion (€30 billion), according to sports business website Sportico, brings fresh questions.

"This deal may have positive economic and social impacts across Africa, but we should be realistic about circumstances on the ground in Rwanda," Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told DW.

"Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One in February 2025 to ask how it is addressing the human rights impacts of its activities, including regarding Rwanda and other countries’ bid to host a F1 Grand Prix. We did not receive a response," said Mudge, adding that F1 should only approve racing in the country after addressing the human rights impacts of hosting a race there.

"Rwanda, like other countries, has also used high-profile sports deals and races in the past to distract from its abysmal human rights record. Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law."

For Mohamed Keita, returning the sport to Africa is overdue, but the choice of country is telling.

"The fact that F1 excluded the world's second largest continent from its race series for three decades is indefensible in its own right and is actually a stain on a sport which claims to be global," Keita, Senior Policy Officer, Africa, at the Human Rights Foundation told DW.

"The choice of Rwanda, however, is deeply controversial," Keita continued. "Rwanda is a brutal dictatorship. Its regime is under partial US sanctions for its military occupations of territories of eastern DRC. Rwanda is arming and financing a militia involved in rapes, massacres, forced recruitment and violent plunder of natural resources."

Formula One has history on the continent. In 1958, there was a race in Morocco and more recently, in South Africa, where the last F1 race in Africa took place at the Kyalami racetrack in Johannesburg in 1993. Many previous races in the country were overshadowed by the policy of apartheid.

Despite Rwanda securing the deal first, South Africa believes it will host before them. When Rwanda announced their hosting, South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa sent his congratulations in a social media post, adding: "This contract is a recognition of the capabilities of the Rwandan nation and of our continent more broadly."

South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie also congratulated Rwanda, but pivotally added that South Africa "will get F1, even before 2030."

There is no denying that hosting a race in South Africa would cost significantly less time and money, given the existing infrastructure.

In either country, comes a legacy opportunity. Sports such as Formula One, where the majority of decision-makers, drivers, team principles and engineers are white men, are a living example of the unlevel playing field. The hope of racing in Africa is that it will go some way to changing that.

"I think that's the kind of aspirational drive of hosting a Formula 1 race. It's leveraging STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] education, technology, aspiring young girls or women, leveling the playing fields, if it's for all those other reasons and we can make it work then I say yes to Formula 1 in Africa," Dr. Kamilla Swart-Arries, an expert in South Africa's events industry and the legacy of sports events, told DW in 2024.

"I hope F1 will consider further investment in developing African talent in motorsport," said Keita. "There's a lot of good that F1 can do if it genuinely wants to grow the sport in Africa, but Rwanda does not make sense at this moment unless you're doing it purely for the benefit of one dictator and the beauty of the hilly terrain."

"The proposition here is to take the world's most expensive sport to Rwanda, which is one of the world's poorest countries. Rwanda is consistently listed among the UN's list of the 25 least developed countries in the world," said Keita.

The return of the fastest show in sports is a huge moment for both Rwanda and Africa. It raises questions about President Kagame's use of sport, but it also offers an opportunity to shape the event's legacy. Unlike the race Rwanda wants to host, this is not about being the fastest but about making the most of the chance.

#1044. Gianni Infantino’s confidential World Cup sell-off documents to be shared with Fifa members

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was rejected by three continental confederations

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Confidential documents linked to Gianni Infantino’s hugely controversial World Cup private investor plan will be made available for members of the Fifa Council to view.

Infantino had sought to set up a company, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the commercial interests of the World Cup and its other competitions, with private investors holding a minority stake.

The plan was abandoned in August after three continental confederations rejected it and Uefa threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions.

A letter sent by Uefa on behalf of European members of the Fifa Council on 19 October demanded answers to a series of questions about FFE and a range of other concerns about Infantino’s presidency by Monday.

It’s understood Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom wrote to all Council members on Monday inviting them to view key documents related to the FFE proposal.

Council members – including Fifa vice-presidents such as Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin – have been invited to register their interest within the next two weeks should they wish to view the documents, in person and under specific conditions, at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich.

The conditions specified are understood to have been applied in order to preserve Fifa’s confidentiality obligations.

For now it is understood the documents to be made available relate solely to FFE. The 19 October letter sought clarity around the Folarin Balogun disciplinary case and a range of other matters, but it is understood a wider response will come to Council members in due course.

Fifa is understood to have viewed Uefa’s two-week deadline to respond to all the 42 areas covered in the letter as unfeasible.

Fifa has been focused on the organisation of the inaugural Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, featuring 189 nations and 3,000 players. It is also preparing for an extraordinary Fifa Congress on 23 November to appoint the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cups.

Uefa’s ongoing legal action in the United States – where it has sought disclosure of documents linked to FFE – is also understood to have created legal boundaries.

The 19 October letter posed questions around the decision to award exclusivity to Thrive Capital to lead the FFE private investor group. Thrive was founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

It also sought answers around the timeline surrounding the plan’s development, the $20bn (£15bn) valuation placed on the company, why Fifa felt it was necessary to seek private investment given its healthy cash reserves and whether Infantino stood to gain personally from the plan.

Council members had attended a meeting of the Fifa Council on 15 October and asked Infantino questions in person. One of those members, Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt, said after the meeting that Council members were asked to submit questions in writing.

The Fifa Council is not due to meet again until 16 December. Uefa has pledged to identify a credible alternative candidate to stand against Infantino in the Fifa presidential election next March.

The deadline for candidacy submissions is 18 November.

Harry Kane’s current contract is due to expire next summer

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Harry Kane expects to sign a new contract with Bayern Munich “within the next few days” after winning the Ballon d’Or last week

The 33-year-old’s current contract is due to expire next summer after he signed a four-year deal when leaving Tottenham in 2023.

There has been speculation over Kane’s future, with some wondering whether he could be tempted back to the Premier League to try to chase down Alan Shearer’s all-time goalscoring record.

However, the England captain is now ready to extend his stay at the Allianz Arena.

“I would say it is more (a matter of) days,” Kane said at a press conference ahead of Tuesday's Champions League match at Atletico Madrid.

"There has been good conversations over this weekend and today as well. I know I keep saying we are close, but we are extremely close now. Details are just details in every contract.

"A lot of the bigger stuff has been ironed out and we are happy with, but in every contract there is loads of little things that go into it, small details that in the end the lawyers have to thrash out and figure out.

“So all in all I would say it is more days than weeks. From what I have heard, the conversations have gone well again today and hopefully we will be in a place to do something within the next few days.”

Last season, Kane scored 73 goals for club and country, while he also won two trophies in Germany and led England to third place at the World Cup.

This ensured that he won the Ballon d’Or, as he became the first Englishman to claim the coveted award since Michael Owen in 2001.

Kane paraded the Ballon d’Or on Saturday, but then missed a second-half penalty and hit the post, as Bayern Munich drew 2-2 with rivals Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga in his first match since last Monday’s award ceremony.

“Hi everyone, I just wanted to say I’m extremely proud to be a FC Bayern Munich player,” Kane told the crowd prior to the game. “The support you have shown me since I arrived has been incredible.”

#1042. Everton beat Newcastle again as 10-man Magpies booed off by own fans after dismal display

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Newcastle 0-1 Everton: The Magpies slipped to their second defeat against Everton in the space of four days

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Everton returned to winning ways in the Premier League as Thierno Barry's second-half goal secured a 1-0 victory against Newcastle at St James' Park.

Following a first half with few clear opportunities, the decisive moment arrived shortly after the restart when Barry poked home his fourth league goal of the campaign.

A frustrating evening for Newcastle worsened in the closing minutes when substitute Jacob Ramsey was shown two quick yellow cards, leaving the hosts with 10 men as they slipped to 13th in the Premier League table. The Magpies were booed off at half time and full time, piling the pressure on manager Matthias Jaissle.

The match took place four days after Everton's 3-1 win over Newcastle in the Carabao Cup fourth round. Both sides made two changes to their line-ups, with Anthony Elanga and Joelinton starting for the Magpies, while Jarrad Branthwaite and Harrison Armstrong came in for the visitors.

Harvey Barnes looked lively on Newcastle's left, curling a shot wide before a looping cross drifted past the far post. Everton goalkeeper Jordan Pickford was then required to collect Will Osula's deflected cross from a tight angle.

Joelinton had an effort blocked by James Tarkowski and Merlin Rohl fired over as both teams sought a breakthrough. James Garner blasted a free-kick into the Newcastle wall, before Barnes forced Pickford to tip the ball over after his cross struck Branthwaite.

Joelinton shot wide from distance before Everton created late first-half chances, with Jake O'Brien failing to head in Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's cross and Harrison Armstrong skewing a shot wide.

The Toffees took the lead four minutes after the interval. A clever pass from a free-kick set Tyrique George free on the left to shoot low at Lukas Hornicek. The ball squeezed under the goalkeeper, allowing Barry to tap in the loose ball after a VAR check for two tight offsides.

Hornicek saved Branthwaite's header as Everton sought a second, while Fabian Schar shot over and Pickford held Joe Willock's header. Hornicek then denied Dewsbury-Hall and saved O'Brien's effort from the resulting corner.

Barnes' cross was almost converted by Elanga, but his shot hit the post and rolled along the line before being cleared. Pickford later punched away a Jacob Murphy corner before Ramsey volleyed wide, with the goalkeeper subsequently denying Yoane Wissa twice.

In eight minutes of added time, Ramsey received his marching orders after picking up two yellow cards in quick succession, concluding a disappointing night for the home side as Everton claimed all three points.

#1041. EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China

At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.

If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation.

Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain.

"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."

Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.

The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.

Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.

Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.

"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."

Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.

However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions.

Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.

"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.

"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."

A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.

Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.

As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.

The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.

However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.

Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.

"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."

Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.

"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.

"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

The Danish legend missed out on his country's only major tournament victory

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 30 years on, Denmark's Euro 92 victory remains one of international football's most remarkable stories.

A team that had failed to qualify for the tournament would eventually go on to lift the trophy, having taken full advantage of Yugoslavia's ejection following the break-up of the country.

Goals from John Jensen and Kim Vilfort sealed a 2-0 win over Germany in the final, with the Danes claiming the stunning victory without one of their greatest-ever players, following Michael Laudrup's decision to walk away from international football two years earlier to focus on his Barcelona career.

The mercurial midfielder had been central to the rise of Danish Dynamite, the thrilling side that reached the semi-finals of Euro 84 before winning over the hearts and minds of so many at the 1986 World Cup. But his decision to prioritise club football meant he would miss Denmark's greatest triumph.

Speaking about the Danish side of the 1980s, Laudrup credited his manager and his team-mates' decision to ply their trade in Europe's best leagues.

"A lot of the players were playing for big clubs in Europe, at a time when not many foreign players were allowed in European leagues," Laudrup tells FourFourTwo. "We had a lot of individual quality. The arrival of Sepp Piontek as manager in 1979 was also pivotal – he fulfilled our potential. We went to the European Championship and beat Yugoslavia 5-0. We had a fantastic game against Belgium too, which we won 3-2 from 2-0 down. In the end, we only lost on penalties in the semi-final against Spain.

"At the 1986 World Cup, we beat Uruguay 6-1 and West Germany 2-0, but then went out against Spain in the last 16. We were 1-0 up, but a poor second half cost us and we lost 5-1. The big countries had tournament experience. We learned from that and could apply it in 1992 and 1998, where we achieved good results in the latter stages."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

And what about his decision to quit the Denmark team in 1990?

"In the second game of qualifying, we drew in Northern Ireland, then we lost at home against Yugoslavia, who had a fantastic team," Laudrup continues. "I realised they’d qualify, even if we beat them away. I was also in the early stages of my time at Barça, which was important to me, and the two teams played completely different football. I wasn’t really happy with the way we played in the national team, but it’s always the manager’s decision. Still, I thought, ‘With this style of play, I can never be the same as at Barcelona.’

"As we weren’t able to qualify, I decided to focus 100 per cent on Barça. Yugoslavia went on to win the group, but because of the war, Denmark were suddenly given their place. People asked me if I wanted to go, but I didn’t want to join at the last moment, even though I could have. I felt it wouldn’t have been fair."

Laudrup would eventually return to the Danish national side in 1993.

"I’d won three league titles and the European Cup with Barça, and every time, they asked if I wanted to go back," he explains. "I’d achieved all the things I wanted with Barcelona, so I agreed. Unfortunately we lost a World Cup qualifier to Spain – the third time they got in our way, after beating us in 1984 and 1986. Spain has given me so much at personal and club level, then it’s curious how much it has taken away from me with the national team! But then we went to Euro 96 and the 1998 World Cup."

His 100th international cap came during the 1998 World Cup, with Laudrup calling time on his international career following their quarter-final defeat to Brazil.

"That was a great stage to retire on," he reflects. "After leaving Real Madrid, I went to Japan – I wanted to go somewhere I could still play, but also have a bit of freedom after being in Southern Europe since 1983. I thought maybe I should retire from the national team, but the coach asked me to continue. I realised that even though I liked life in Japan, I wanted to finish at a higher level. There was some interest from countries like Turkey and France – Marseille wanted me – but the Southern European passion was what I didn’t want any more! [Laughs]

"I joined Ajax – that team was incredible, with the De Boer brothers, Danny Blind, Edwin van der Sar and Jari Litmanen. We won the Double, so I continued with the national team, we qualified for the World Cup and lost in the quarter-finals to Brazil. We really challenged them and it was a great way to finish my career."

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1039. The ‘magical night’ Man United must replicate to halt slide into chaos

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

With a fractured dressing room and fans in open revolt, the beleaguered head coach needs a result against Roma akin to their 2007 triumph to arrest the club’s decline

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

When the Champions League draw pitted Manchester United against Roma, the more nostalgic were transported back 20 seasons. To a night that, ultimately, proved a staging post on Sir Alex Ferguson’s way to conquering Europe the following season. To a European Cup win that, in its margin, has only been bettered in United’s history by the Busby Babes’ 10-0 demolition of Anderlecht in 1956. To the only time in 464 appearances for United that Michael Carrick scored twice.

In 2007, United faced a Roma side that included the World Cup winners Francesco Totti and Daniele de Rossi. They thrashed them 7-1. “A magical night,” Carrick recalled. “It was one of the best nights, one of the best games, one of the best atmospheres I've been fortunate enough to witness. So the fact that I scored a couple and that was very unusual gives me great, great memories, but it was more the actual whole the emotion of the night. It was a special one.”

But Carrick’s initial response had been: “Long time ago, hey?” Increasingly, that comment could be applied to many of the good times: to the heady days in spring when he won 12 of his first 17 games after returning to Old Trafford. Now, nine without a win, beaten in each of the last three, Carrick could do with recapturing some of the magic he and his teammates produced to inflict Roma’s record European defeat. Although, as Gian Piero Gasperini’s team are third in Serie A and, two weeks ago, United lost 4-1 to the side now fourth in the Italian top flight, it feels unlikely. But, almost two decades ago, United had lost consecutive games before welcoming Roma to Old Trafford. Things can change, quickly and dramatically.

“You might think I'm crazy with the results we've had and what's going on, but I genuinely, really can't wait for the game,” said Carrick. And indeed, it may sound delusional; or, at the least, the words of a man who remembers what United was and imagines it could be again.

But not, perhaps, with him as manager, or this group of players, or this hierarchy or these owners. Carrick’s cryptic reference to “what’s going on” was shorthand for the public criticisms of either him or Jason Wilcox voiced by Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez, of the Argentinian’s sending-off at Chelsea, of the fans’ audible dissent against the sporting director, the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, of the possibility this is his last week in the job.

“I can’t look into the future,” said Carrick. “You never know what's going to happen.” Lose to Roma and then Aston Villa and his position would seem untenable; but then it did when United were beaten by Bournemouth last Sunday and he was given a stay of execution.

But too few of Carrick’s squad seem intent on keeping him. The feckless Martinez, whose recklessness ensured defeat on Sunday, is a case in point and, after a series of wretched performances, Carrick faces a decision whether to select the Argentinian. It is his way to defend his players and he said: “I've got no concerns about [his] commitment at all. The dressing room is a good, good place, so perceptions are a funny thing.”

The loyalists, the men still in Carrick’s camp, definitely include Kobbie Mainoo, who has known the older midfielder he was 14 and the former United captain was beginning his coaching career. Carrick revived Mainoo’s fortunes, after Ruben Amorim had marginalised him, when he took temporary charge in January. “I’m grateful for the trust the boss has put in me,” he said. “Knowing he's a player who's been at this club and knows the history of this club and knows what it takes to win, I take those words to heart.”

It may be a rare speck of good news for Carrick that Mainoo returned from injury as a substitute at Chelsea. United have only lost one game the Mancunian has started this season.

Mainoo said the players appreciate Carrick’s tactic of trying to shield them from criticism. He knows that they owe him. “Of course,” he said. “And I feel like our way to repay that is to be behind the manager on the pitch and off it, and fight for us and fight for us as a team.”

The supporters have made it clear where their allegiances lie, serenading Carrick and booing the players after Bournemouth’s emphatic win, and Mainoo reflected: “In these tough times you can't expect the fans 100,000 percent of the time to be to be happy and cheering when we're not putting out results.”

Which they have not been. There could be consequences, and not merely for Carrick. The 2008 Champions League winner played in three finals of this competition. Now United have lost their last two European matches and their next five – Roma, Sporting CP, Leipzig, Bayern Munich and Villarreal – offer few guarantees of victory for a stumbling side. United risk becoming the first Premier League club to fail to even get a top-24 finish in this revamped format. “There is the bigger picture and it is about getting through to the later stages,” said Carrick.

As he knows, United once surged into a Champions League semi-final with a 7-1 demolition. But that was a long time ago.

#1038. Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter

She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

In the history of German resistance to Nazism, some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl, Claus von Stauffenberg, Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser. Yet many others have remained largely forgotten.

Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp.

Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16.

"Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," said cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok."

Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic.

But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance.

According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler."

"She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," noted Weltz-Rombach.

Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery.

Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935.

After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew.

In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive.

She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered.

Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism.

Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler.

They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger, said Weltz-Rombach. That the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books, she added.

Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia.

According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto.

In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year.

Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany.

"There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," said Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance."

The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures, a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity.

Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners.

Since Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate.

These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explained Weltz-Rombach.

"Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be."

"[Women's] resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," said Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." Other examples include a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters.

Even though many of the eyewitnesses are now dead, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched."

#1037. Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

The former Liverpool defender has been a Sky Sports regular for more than a decade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Immediately after hanging up his boots, Jamie Carragher moved into the media world, with Sky Sports signing up the former Liverpool and England defender at the start of the 2013/14 season.

Over the past 13 years, Carragher has become of the most recognisable and distinct voices in football broadcasting, whether that was sparring with Gary Neville on Monday Night Football back in the day, or showing his lighter side on shows such as Stick to Football.

But how does he assess his own evolution from player to pundit? And how does he compare himself with his former on-pitch rival Neville?

“There are parts of understanding football where Gary’s on a completely different level to me – his understanding of how the leagues work, or the EFL,” Carragher tells FourFourTwo, referencing Neville’s role as co-owner of League Two club Salford City.

“He’s in meetings because he’s an owner, and he had a really good take on things like Covid, when there was no football going on, and also things like a football regulator and how deals are done, whereas I don’t. He’s an authority on subjects like that. And he’s also the authority on winning the Premier League – I have to accept that.”

For Carragher, research, preparation and tactical insight is where he excels in front of camera – even if on a show such as Stick to Football, that can get overshadowed by a witty one-liner from someone else on the panel. “It can be a little frustrating,” Carragher smiles.

“But that’s the nature of the show. If I make a point, then someone comes out with, ‘It’s just 11 vs 11, it’s just 22 men kicking the ball around’, you can think, ‘What’s f**king the point in anything!’”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For Carragher, though, it’s this detail and alternative ways of analysing the game that keeps him engaged.

“But everybody sees the game in a different way, and I love the details – that’s what gets my juices flowing,” he continues. “Finding something or a bit of analysis that no one else has seen.

“A lot of the time there are these myths in football, about things that happened years ago, but when you actually look at the detail, they didn’t f**king happen!”

Given his love for detail, how does Carragher view this stage of his career in football, compared to his playing days? “I was a very good player, but I’m a great pundit,” he jokes.

“Modest!” laughs Neville, sat beside him. “As for me, I always said that on my tombstone, it would say ‘Six out of 10’. I like the idea of being consistent.

“I don’t think I’m better as a pundit or player, I think I’m consistent.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1035. The baffling question surrounding Unai Emery and Aston Villa ahead of Barcelona showdown

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Emery has worked wonders at Villa Park, with a Champions League trip to Camp Nou the latest reward, but where his managerial future lies continues to be a topic of debate

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It is the biggest club from England’s second city against the biggest from Spain’s. And if the similarities between Birmingham and Barcelona may end there – the Brummie separatist movement is rather less prominent that its Catalan counterpart, for instance – then a trip to Camp Nou is both a sign of a new eminence and part of a broader question about Aston Villa’s status.

In footballing terms, England’s second city has often tended to be Manchester, Liverpool or London. The notion that Villa will forever lie further down the footballing food chain seemed to underpin Jamie Carragher’s somewhat derogatory comments last week; even if Villa’s threat to sue the pundit, signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris, struck many as frankly silly.

Meanwhile, Unai Emery wore his Villa blazer to the Ballon d’Or ceremony last week. It could be interpreted as a gesture of his enduring loyalty, amid the possibility the Manchester United job will become vacant; but perhaps he simply liked the garment.

Whichever, Villa may have one of the two finest managers currently working in the Premier League, along with Emery’s fellow Basque Mikel Arteta, and one of the best in Europe; his record five Europa League wins indicates as much. Villa’s renaissance has been inspired by Emery and can feel reliant upon him.

They could be a club who are establishing themselves as a regular presence on such nights or one who may not been seen again at Camp Nou for decades; in March, Newcastle, like Villa now, in a second Champions League campaign in three seasons, lost 7-2 to Barcelona. It remains to be seen if they will return any time soon.

For Villa, this is a first game against Barcelona at their iconic stadium for 43 years, since a Super Cup defeat; Villa were European champions then and won the second leg 3-0. It was their last continental trophy until Emery’s side beat Freiburg in May.

Villa are ticking off the clashes with the European superpowers. Two years ago, they renewed acquaintances with Bayern Munich and, as they did in the 1982 European Cup final, beat them 1-0. They ran Paris Saint-Germain close in the 2025 quarter-finals, only narrowly lost to them in this summer’s Super Cup and face them again next month. It only really leaves Real Madrid of the current elite to face.

For Emery, a return to his native Spain can serve as a reminder that he has never been hired by any of their three major forces. Atletico Madrid can at least offer the reason that Diego Simeone has been in situ for 15 years. Real may feel that Emery’s obsessive attention to detail may not be suited to their superstars or that his relative lack of charisma may not work at the Bernabeu. Barcelona tend to look for managers who fit into their traditions and suit their tactics. Emery’s sides are often entertaining, but he did not study at the school of tiki-taka.

Instead, he punched above his weight with other clubs in his homeland. He finished third in LaLiga three times with Valencia, won a hat-trick of Europa Leagues with Sevilla and a fourth with Villarreal.

He became the master of knockout competitions; indeed Emery has won three Europa Leagues since Barcelona last won the Champions League. And yet a competition Villa were knocked out of showed their priorities in their new reality. A heavily weakened side exited the Carabao Cup at Bournemouth last week; Emery has his sights on grander targets. After three straight wins, Villa could be on course for another top-eight group-stage finish in the Champions League.

Meanwhile, as the ‘big six’ looks an increasingly anachronistic term, the changing landscape of English football offers the chance for Villa to be frequent top-five finishers in the immediate future. Remarkably, the last English club outside the supposedly big six to play in the European Cup or Champions League, excluding qualifiers, in consecutive seasons is Villa themselves: between 1981 and 1983, entering the competition in the second season as holders.

So Emery’s reign could assume historic proportions, and not merely at Villa Park. And in that respect, one of the biggest games in Villa’s history may only be the second largest of their week.

Their trip to Old Trafford on Sunday may be framed by the discussions about Michael Carrick, his possible successors, arguably the best qualified of all, in Emery, and perhaps the favourite, in Eddie Howe. Whereas Howe concluded he could not develop a second terrific team with Newcastle, there are encouraging signs that Emery can with Villa. If he has a decision to make, that might shape it.

And a comparison of Villa and United now, whether in terms of the starting 11s, the direction of travel, the Premier League table or the Champions League table, could show a shift in the balance of power. Villa certainly looks the more appealing prospect. But for some, the question may be not why he does not go to United, but why Spain’s big three don’t come in for him.

#1033. What tech entrepreneurs can teach scientists about failure

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Mary Ryan discusses what industry can teach academia about failure in science. Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Are universities doing enough to help students learn from their mistakes, and allowing them to see setbacks as a spur to creativity and success?

Materials scientist Mary Ryan, Vice-Provost (Research and Enterprise) at Imperial College London, argues that a good training in science should accommodate learning from setbacks, wrong moves and false starts.

Too often, students judge themselves harshly by one poor exam result or failed experiment, she suggests.

In April 2026 Ryan addressed Failure in Science, a conference held at Imperial in partnership with Nature. In the third episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, she says: “People often point to California’s Bay Area as being this hotbed of innovation.

“You can very easily be a serial startup creator there. When you talk to entrepreneurs, one of the first things they tell you is the three companies that they had that failed. That doesn’t preclude them starting a new one and getting funding for it, whereas I think in the UK and probably in Europe in general, there’s more of a requirement for a track record.

“We have to shift that dynamic if the rest of the world is going to catch up with what’s happening in the US.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03485-2

I’m Dr. Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

And in episode three of Failure in Science, a podcast series about how to do science better, we explore failure and institutions.

Yes, we all have our personal failures, our bad times.

But what if it is actually our institutions that are failing us?

What if a rigid system of education is stifling our imagination?

What if the hunt for grants makes us play safe and narrows our thinking?

Jem Woods, who’s a professor at Imperial College London, opened the Failure in Science conference in April with a quote from Albert Einstein:

The quote is, “As our circle of knowledge expands, so does the circumference of darkness surrounding it. And we have to continue to keep on thinking around and being critically reflective on that uncertainty and the parameters of that uncertainty and how we perceive what we know and what we don’t know.”

And I think that sits at the heart of the failure in science questions.

Yes, I’m Mary Ryan. I’m the Vice Provost for Research and Enterprise at Imperial College London, and I’m the Armourers and Brasiers’ Chair for material science.

So what would I say my big failures are? When you see someone who’s clearly, you know, a successful academic?

You know, I have a research group at Imperial College, so in some ways, I’ve been very successful.

And I think it’s hard, particularly for early career researchers, to see people who have you know, quotes, “made it,” reflecting that they had failures.

So I think actually it’s really important that we talk about things that we weren’t successful at.

Every academic has got a folder on their computer of proposals that were rejected, papers that were rejected for one reason or other.

That doesn’t mean those ideas weren’t worthy or valuable.

Some of them were bad, and we had to be told they were bad.

But how you respond to that rejection? I think failure and rejection are intimately entwined, right?

And that shapes who you are as a scientist, actually, how, that you get them, but how you respond to them.

But there are many times where you do an experiment with a certain focus, and that experiment itself might fail, or you miss something in the background.

Famously, in the 1980s and early 90s, everybody that was working on surface science STM. Many surface science approaches would use highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) as a standard substrate.

To make your surface clean, what we did, we’d use a piece of tape. We cleave the surface because graphite cleaves very nicely, as we know.

For about 10 years, literally thousands of people were throwing away bits of graphene on their Sellotape because we were focused on the surface and not what we’d done to clean the surface.

And of course the discovery of graphene using exactly that technique was awarded the Nobel Prize.

And I think that’s just a really interesting reflection that you can be doing a certain piece of work and that is successful, but sometimes you’ve also thrown away what was important.

I think that’s a metaphor for life, probably. By focusing on one thing, you throw away what’s really important.

So at the conference, Professor Jem Woods quoted Einstein’s discussion around the kind of, the circumference of knowledge and what is known and what is not known.

And it’s really challenging from an educational training perspective to get that balance of supporting students to understand what we know, but also understanding that there’s uncertainty at the boundaries of that knowledge.

It’s challenging because that makes assessment more difficult. And there’s a large degree of assessment built into how we teach and train and educate people.

But it’s difficult because it becomes very uncomfortable for both the educator and the student to deal with a space where we just don’t know.

Now, I actually think it’s a brilliant opportunity for thinking about how we design education to really put some of those challenging questions into the hands and minds of students, because I think it’s when there are “What are the big questions of the universe?”

You know, they’ve inspired people for generations. And we’ve still got them.

There’s a danger that we now treat education and knowledge as complete when it’s not. And that means that you’re probably not lighting some of those sparks that we’ve seen before.

I think it’s also really, really important that in a space where knowledge is also increasingly captured and categorized by AI, that there’s a real understanding of people that we train that we don’t have the sum total of knowledge.

We don’t know everything. There’s still uncertainties. There’s still questions.

So you’ve also got to question (when you interact with frontier technology) about what if the knowledge you are being told, what knowledge it has been trained on, what is the boundary of that knowledge as well?

So all of those things mean we have to, I think, bring it further into the centre, what is unknown, before we build on what we do know.

So science is founded on experimentation and with the risk of failure fundamentally at its core.

I’m really, curious, I guess, about the balance between applied science and curiosity-driven, sometimes called fundamental science.

And yet, I wonder, aren’t we all curious? And isn’t it that we all want to be curious?

Isn’t that what drives experimentation and testing and knowledge and knowledge generation?

We’re constantly thinking about narrowing our boundaries.

How do we set our boundaries? And yet, we should always be thinking about how we expand our boundaries, how we remain curious.

Professor Jem Woods made an interesting point at the conference around expanding knowledge and this kind, a bit of a tension between discovery, applied science, and how we think about experimentation in that space.

One of the things I like to just try to take everything back to is when you’re thinking about science and applied science, what are the questions you are asking?

Are you asking a why question? Are you asking a what question? Are you asking a how question?

Because that sort of shapes what kind of an experiment you would design and think about.

If you were to take a, you know, a big step back and think about you know pushing the boundary of discovery science, which are often why questions.

And you have a hypothesis or an idea about you know what the answer is to the why, you should always design your experiment to disprove that hypothesis, right?

That’s the way that science actually progresses.

So you should be designing experiments in some ways that fail, right?

Because you’re testing to get to disprove a hypothesis.

I feel like we’ve lost a little bit of that because those experiments are hard to do. They’re hard to think about. They’re hard to publish.

And so what are the mechanisms, by the way, we capture those disproving of hypotheses as really parts of contribution to knowledge.

Because they narrow down what are the right answers and what are the right ways forward.

I still think we need to make sure we capture that as a really fundamental part of the scientific method when we’re doing our training of students.

But quite often, if you want to really, but again, push the boundaries of what you’re going to be able to deliver, you have to work out where those boundaries are, right?

So you have to get to the point where something doesn’t work to understand what does work.

And I think all of those are places where you start to see, and I’m slightly using works and doesn’t work as a failure version, which is not quite the same.

But I think it’s important that you get to the point when you’ve pushed it as far as you can, the frontier of discovery or applied science.

I’m Roseanne. So I’ve been at Imperial for around four years now.

So I think the failure in education session was very relevant to me because I’ve lived it.

So what I really thought was quite inquisitive was this tension between systemic and individual failure, and how the system might, kind of, create individual failure, but then individual failure can kind of symbolize this systemic failure too.

But I felt that what was really important was to make known to students that failure always carries loads of weight and symbolism within our day-to-day lives, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that we’ve failed.

So during the final plenary session, Rosanne I think, fed back on the failure in education.

And she talked really interestingly about the difference between systemic and individual failures.

And I feel like the failure in education discussion really symbolized this first step towards acknowledging, number one, that education is kind of underpinned by inequalities.

That means that other people might not have the right science capital or kind of social capital to mean that we all carry the same equal understanding of science, and that means that we need to bridge these gaps.

But also at the same time that we need to fulfill students with confidence to be able to, not fail, but to make mistakes that result in improving and acknowledging that failure isn’t failure as we like to symbolize it, but how it drives you towards creating....

One thing that really resonated with me and what she was talking about was this idea that at an individual level, the impact of failure is not equally felt.

And the likelihood of failure is not equal, depending on your social capital, your background, the disparity that we have in educational inputs, and the disparity that failure or perceived failure has on your educational outputs, and your life chances.

And this is a really big challenge for all of us, I think, to deal with as a society and as an education community, how do we level that playing field on the way in, and make sure that we are enabling the brightest people, wherever they come from, with a background, to be able to have an equal chance of success?

But then also on the other side of that, some people are allowed to fail, and still succeed, right? And we know we all recognize that in life. We all have experiences of that.

One of the things I think this is it really incumbent on educational establishments is to think about building resilience.

Right, building resilience in our students so they don’t feel that a single failure of a single exam is a reflection on the totality of what they bring, on their talent and their knowledge and what they’ve been learning.

That actually, it’s seen as a space for increased learning, a space to reflect and go back and say, “Actually I can do better.”

Of course, we live and our systems, I think it’s where it comes to the systemic part. Our systems are built on a, you know, pass fail first two one.

And I think what we need to reflect a little bit on is how we talk about that.

I mean, I think you know I am I am still a believer that we need to train people to the highest level they can, and we need to say that we are bringing the brightest and the best, and giving them as the best education they can, in order that they can go on and change the world, right?

But how do we say within this pool of people, everybody is valuable, and everybody’s contribution is valuable, and your output is going to go on and make a difference.

I guess thinking about why it’s important that we actually embrace the idea of failure has got many, many different reasons in it within a university and education context.

One is, I think, the perception of what success looks like for an early career researcher.

There is still a lingering, if you start off doing research, the ultimate endpoint view is to be an academic professor.

We know the likelihood of that is probably about 5%.

But also we know they’re not necessarily the most impactful jobs, right?

And so one thing that we’ve been doing at Imperial is establishing a new research institute for early career researchers that helps them see multiple pathways.

So what does it look like to have a job in industry? What does it look like to work in policy? To work in publishing? To work in the public sector?

And then think about what are the steps that might get you to those kind of careers very early on, not as a second choice, but as actually “That’s my north star from day one. This is what I want to do with my research.”

And that’s an important reset on expectations and the expectations that you give yourself and the expectations that we, as an organization, give to early career researchers that are here.

The other area I think is really important is on innovation and entrepreneurship.

Those are inherently areas that are high risk.

They should be high risk, and they should be, you know, we talk about failing fast.

What we also find is that when you’re in an academic culture, students don’t like to fail.

You know, you don’t want to fail an exam, you don’t want to fail a test.

So, what we’ve done with our entrepreneurship for our undergraduate programme, we’ve set that up through an entity we call the Enterprise Lab.

We have programmes that train students to think about entrepreneurship, how to bring an idea and turn it into a device or a company.

We link them to entrepreneurs outside of the university.

All of that is deliberately extracurricular, right? So it’s not counted for credit.

They can come in, they can explore their ideas. They can be stupid ideas. They can be brilliant ideas.

But they’re not in a framework where someone’s going to give them an A or a B or a C. They’re going to say, “Did I make a company? Did I not make a company? Did I decide I want to do that? I didn’t want to do that.”

And so it completely changes the culture of how they. Approach that activity, and that’s really important for it to be almost like a safe space to fail.

Or almost a place where failing is one of the positive outcomes because you’ve done something that was disruptive and it didn’t work, and that’s a good outcome.

And now you take that and you take it back to somewhere else.

So creating that culture of, you know, have an idea, try something, fail fast. No consequences other than you learnt something, right?

It’s a really important part of how we think about entrepreneurship.

What are the systems questions around innovation spinouts and failure?

People often point to the to the Bay Area, the US, as being this hotbed of innovation, and one of the reasons for that is you can very easily be a serial startup creator, and you have a startup then it fails, and a startup then it fails.

And in fact, when you talk to entrepreneurs in the Bay Area, one of the first things they tell you is the three companies that they had that failed.

That doesn’t preclude them starting a new one and getting funding for it, whereas I think in the UK and probably in Europe in general, there’s more of a requirement for a track record.

So people who have had multiple startups, typically they’ve all succeeded, right?

And so it’s this difference between at a systems level, how you perceive that failure as being “Well, this is my only one chance, so I’ve got to make it work,“ versus, “I’m going to try three or four times until that one works."

We have to shift that dynamic if the rest of the world is going to catch up with what’s happening in the US.

That means a few things. It means probably more venture capital, venture capital is able to take more risk, but also again that resilience in our individuals.

That if this one thing doesn’t work, they should try again and try again.
